_comment: THE ARTIFACT CONTRACT: what must be true of EVERY shipped busbar binary, as DATA.
Owner, 2026-08-08: "should just be 1 build pipeline that takes what its building: arm, windows,
mac, but it does the same thing for each no way for 1 to be different", and "100% or 0% for
each build".
WHY THIS IS A FILE AND NOT A SEQUENCE OF `run:` STEPS. Through 1.5.3 every property a release
binary was supposed to have was asserted on the INPUT side -- an env var set on a build step --
and never on the OUTPUT. `BUSBAR_RELEASE_PUBKEY` was set on both build steps, the workflow was
green, a comment in release.yml stated the key was baked in, and
busbar-aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu 1.5.3 shipped with no key at all: `option_env!` is a
COMPILE-time read that fails silently to `None`. Setting an env var says what was intended.
Only inspecting the shipped bytes says what happened.
Because the rows are data, adding a property is ONE ENTRY here plus its check function in
scripts/verify-artifact.py, and it then applies to every target automatically -- there is no
per-target list to forget a platform in, which is how the aarch64 leg went three releases
without a key. scripts/verify-artifact.py asserts SET EQUALITY between the ids declared here
and the checks it implements, so a row added here with no implementation is a hard failure
rather than a silently-skipped property, and an implementation with no row here is too.
scripts/tests/test_verify_artifact.py additionally requires every row to own BOTH a RED
fixture it flags and a GREEN twin it passes: a row nobody has watched fail is not a row.
`applies_when` is the ONLY way a row may be conditional, it is matched against the target's
own declaration in .github/release-targets.json, and a row that applies to a target CANNOT be
skipped for any other reason -- there is no waiver field and no exception list. Every target
now builds and verifies on a NATIVE runner, so `exec: true` rows run for every platform,
Windows included; nothing is statically approximated because a runner could not execute it.
`min_rows` is a floor. A loop over a discovered set with no floor is a check that passes
without executing: an empty or truncated contract file would otherwise verify every artifact
against nothing and report green.

rows.title: the archive contains exactly the declared executable, at a plausible size
why: GitHub creates an asset row the moment an upload starts, so a truncated or empty upload
lists identically to a good one, and an archive that unpacks to the wrong name (or to a
directory) breaks install.sh and the documented `tar -xzf && ./busbar` in the same silent
way a missing asset does. Assert the members, not the presence.

rows.title: architecture, object format and linkage are what the target declares
why: An asset named `aarch64` that contains x86_64 bytes is 100% broken for everyone who
downloads it, and it is invisible to every check that only executes the binary on the
runner that built it. Parsed straight out of the ELF/Mach-O/PE headers so the check is one
implementation on all three operating systems rather than `file` here and `ldd` there.
The linkage half is a declared property of the target and a row that applies to every
artifact, not an `ldd | grep` in one workflow. Every shipped busbar binary is `dynamic` by
design (W17): a binary that cannot dlopen cannot load a dropped-in plugin, and a static musl
binary cannot dlopen. WHICH libraries it may depend on is `runtime_deps`, below.

rows.title: the release public key is embedded in the shipped bytes
why: THE 1.5.3 DEFECT, ASSERTED ON THE ARTIFACT. busbar-aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu shipped with
no embedded key in 1.5.1, 1.5.2 and 1.5.3 while the other four assets had one. On ARM Linux
-- Graviton, Raspberry Pi, ARM containers -- every correctly-signed first-party plugin was
refused, and the only workaround was `plugins.trust.allow_unsigned: true`, which switches
the requirement off rather than trusting first-party selectively.
This row is the cheap static half: the 64-hex public key must appear verbatim in the binary.
`first_party_plugin` is the half that proves it is the RIGHT key and that it works.

rows.title: the real signed first-party plugin probe reaches its declared state (ready, or the named refusal of a 1.5.x plugin)
why: Functional, not a grep. The plugin is a REAL release of a REAL first-party plugin repo,
downloaded and handed to the SHIPPED binary, whose --list-plugins row must reach the state
release-targets.json's plugin_probe declares. `ready`: `SIGNATURE: first-party` and
`STATUS: ready` -- the proof the embedded key verifies the signatures the plugin repos
produce (run against the real 1.5.3 aarch64 asset it reports, verbatim: `SIGNATURE: unsigned
STATUS: SKIPPED: manifest claims first-party publisher 'busbar' but this build embeds no
busbar release key`). `refused`: an `INVALID:` row carrying every named refusal string --
the probe in force is store-sqlite v1.0.4, a 1.5.x JSON-contract plugin (store abi_version
2), and 1.6.0 loads no legacy plugin (BUSBAR-1.6.0.md THE DESIGN §11.8), so a binary that
reports it `ready` is RED.
The check also asserts `plugins.enabled: true` and a non-empty inventory in the output,
because --list-plugins falls back to the DEFAULT plugins block with a mere [warn] when the
config is unreadable, and a naive check would then read `no plugin tarballs found` and see
no failure text at all.

rows.title: --version reports exactly the version being released
why: ANCHORED on both ends. A substring or prefix match lets `1.5.4` be satisfied by `1.5.40`,
and lets a stale binary from a previous matrix leg pass while claiming to be this release.
The bytes must run and identify themselves as this exact version, nothing more.

rows.title: the documented quickstart boots this binary and answers on /healthz
why: The minimal config.yaml from docs/getting-started.md, the documented default listen address,
and the documented `curl localhost:8080/healthz` -> `ok`. A new user's first five minutes,
run against the artifact they will actually download. This used to be checked for exactly
ONE platform -- verify-deploy.yml hardcodes busbar-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz -- which
is the same shape of gap as the missing key: a property established on one artifact and
assumed for the rest.

rows.title: the build-provenance attestation verifies against these exact bytes
why: `gh attestation verify <archive> --repo GetBusbar/busbar` is the command the docs tell users
to run, so it is the command that must be proven to pass -- on the bytes downloaded from the
release, not on a local copy of the file the build step happened to still have. An
attestation that covers a different digest than the asset a user downloads is worse than
none, because it looks like provenance.
Gated on `published`: an artifact packaged into an image rather than
uploaded has no release asset to attest against, and a row that cannot
run must not be quietly satisfied.

rows.title: the build's own evidence is bound to the shipped bytes by digest
why: The build step records the SHA-256 of the archive it produced. This row asserts that digest
equals the digest of the archive that was actually downloaded from the release. Without it
every evidence-based row below is unanchored: a build could report a verified PGO profile
for bytes that never reached the release, which is a certificate for the wrong artifact.

rows.title: PGO really was applied where the target declares it
why: scripts/pgo-build.sh writes its proof marker ONLY after a non-empty merged profile fed a
successful -Cprofile-use build. This row turns that marker into a contract row rather than
an assertion living in one workflow step: the marker must exist, be marked verified, name
THIS target, and record a non-zero merged-profile size and .profraw count -- and it is bound
to the shipped archive's digest by `build_evidence`, so it certifies these bytes and not
some other build's.
`applies_when` is checked against .github/release-targets.json, and that file carries a
`pgo_floor` scripts/tests/test_release_contract.py enforces, so a target cannot quietly flip `pgo` to false to
make this row stop applying to it.

rows.title: the binary needs nothing at run time beyond the OS's own C runtime
why: W17, THE LINKING DESIGN, ASSERTED ON THE BYTES. Every shipped binary can dlopen a dropped-in
plugin (KICKOFF: every plugin works compiled-in OR dropped-in), so none is a static musl
binary: musl's static libc answers every dlopen with `Dynamic loading not supported`. Every
OTHER dependency (TLS, crypto, jemalloc, the Rust std) is linked in, so the only runtime
requirement is the operating system's own C runtime and loader:
ELF    DT_NEEDED is a subset of `elf_allowed`, and the newest GLIBC_x.y symbol version the
binary needs is at most the target's declared `glibc_max` -- the baseline it runs
on. A build on a newer glibc silently raises the floor (ubuntu-24.04 links
GLIBC_2.39), which is invisible until a user on an older distro runs it.
Mach-O every LC_*_DYLIB is in `macho_allowed`: libSystem, the one library Apple supports
linking dynamically and the most static a macOS binary can be.
PE     no import names a C runtime DLL (`pe_denied_prefixes`): the MSVC build is
+crt-static, so no Visual C++ Redistributable or UCRT install is needed. The
plugin memory ABI never frees across the module boundary (each side frees what it
allocated), which is what makes one CRT per module safe.
Read from the binary's own headers, like `binary_format`, so it runs on any verifier host.

rows.title: the shipped binary dlopens a dropped-in plugin and boots on it
why: Functional, not a header read. The verifier is handed a stub plugin built for this target
by scripts/release/dropin-probe.sh (the in-tree stub store, its dropped-in door, packed
unsigned), drops it into an absolute plugins.dir, names it as `store.module`, and requires
the shipped binary to boot and answer `/healthz`. A configured store that cannot load is a
boot refusal, so `ok` means the library was opened, its door bound and its store opened.
Nothing else in this contract ever dlopens: `first_party_plugin` stops at the manifest ABI
check, which runs BEFORE dlopen, and --list-plugins never loads. Without this row a binary
that cannot load any plugin (a static musl build) passes every other row.

rows.why: busbar 1.5.3's image did NOT boot under any documented invocation: USER 65532:65532 against a root-owned /etc/busbar, so the overlay backend was unwritable and boot refused. The build was green and nothing ran the image. This row runs it.
the image ships a non-root UID deliberately; a fix that restores boot by running as root would trade a boot failure for a privilege regression and look identical in CI.
the same embedded-key property the binaries owe, read from the bytes inside the image rather than inferred from the tarball it should be packaging.
anchored so 1.5.4 cannot be satisfied by 1.5.40, and read from the running image rather than from the tag that labels it.

why: the binary INSIDE the image must be byte-identical to the linux-gnu release artifact the single
build path produced for it. This is what makes the image a PACKAGE rather than a
second build: without it the image could be assembled from a differently-built
binary and every other row would still pass — which is how one artifact came to
embed the plugin release key while its sibling did not. Since W17 the image packages the
SAME published linux-gnu binary a user downloads, on a glibc base, so the image and the
tarball are one artifact.
`dropin_loads`, inside the image. Until W17 the image was FROM scratch around a static musl
binary, which cannot dlopen, so no dropped-in plugin could ever load in the container, and
nothing noticed because no row ever loaded one there. The verifier mounts the same stub
plugin and a config naming it, runs the image, and requires it to reach `listening`.
